title: Lattice Health - Dedicated technical deep dive (rollouts, A/B testing, release notes)
summary: Lattice Health Systems met with Redwood (TAM + SE + Release Eng) for a Dedicated-focused technical deep dive on model version pinning, rollout controls (canary and A/B), rollback mechanics, and how customer-visible release notes are generated from model promotions. Lattice emphasized regulated/healthcare expectations: change visibility, auditability (who/what/when), and clear guidance when a model update could affect output or compliance. Redwood walked through how model metadata v1 and changelog generation map to promotions, how Dedicated rollouts differ from Hosted, and how release notes avoid leaking internal details while still being actionable for customers. Next steps include enabling a sandbox account to preview the Console release notes feed, sharing a sample changelog artifact, and aligning on deprecation timelines and approval workflow for production promotions.
topics: Dedicated deployment model: capacity isolation, throughput predictability, and rollout controls
Model version pinning vs “latest” behavior and what changes trigger a promotion event
A/B testing and canary rollouts: policy configuration, traffic splits, and guardrails
Rollback: instant routing rollback vs full runtime rollback; blast radius considerations
Release notes generation: event-driven changelog, categories (breaking/perf/quality/bugfix/deprecation/security)
Public vs internal fields: redaction rules, RBAC, and what customers see in Console vs support/admin
Audit logs and retention expectations for regulated environments
questions: Can we pin to a specific model version for production while allowing canaries to test a newer version?
If a model is promoted, does that automatically change our Dedicated endpoint, or is it opt-in?
How does Redwood define a breaking change for a model update (tokenization changes, tool calling behavior, output format drift)?
What’s the fastest rollback path if our clinicians report output drift?
Can release notes include eval evidence or at least a high-level quality signal without overstating significance?
Do you provide per-account change history (what changed for us specifically) vs global model release notes?
action_items: Liam O'Rourke (Redwood) - Send Lattice a sample Dedicated rollout policy config and screenshots of the Console release notes + per-model change history views - Due 2025-10-10
Jada Williams (Redwood) - Share a redacted example of a generated changelog artifact for a model promotion (public + internal sections) - Due 2025-10-11
Connor O'Brien (Redwood) - Confirm how CI release note preview/approval gates apply when Lattice requests a custom promotion window for Dedicated - Due 2025-10-14
Mark Liu (Lattice) - Provide Lattice’s current rollout expectations (change window, approvals, rollback RTO) and which models are in scope for the pilot - Due 2025-10-15
Priya Natarajan (Lattice) - Share audit log retention and SIEM export requirements (Splunk vs Sentinel) and whether per-event actor identity is mandatory - Due 2025-10-15
next_steps: Redwood to provision a Dedicated pilot workspace for Lattice with version pinning enabled and a release-notes feed visible in Console (RBAC-scoped).
Schedule a follow-up working session to review Lattice’s desired rollout policy (canary duration, traffic split steps, automated fallback criteria).

transcript:
Meeting: Lattice Health - Dedicated technical deep dive (rollouts, A/B testing, release notes)
Recorded: 2025-10-08 17:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes

Attendees
- Redwood: Liam O'Rourke (TAM), Jada Williams (Staff Eng, Rollouts/Change Visibility), Connor O'Brien (Release Eng)
- Lattice: Alyssa Grant (Director, Platform Eng), Mark Liu (Staff MLOps), Priya Natarajan (Security/Compliance), Sam Ortega (Product)


[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the deep dive we said we’d do on Dedicated rollouts, A/B, version pinning, and how the release notes tie to model promotions. Jada is gonna drive most of the technical bits. Connor’s here for the release process, like how things get published.

[00:18] Alyssa Grant: Great. Yeah, we want to understand the mechanics, not just the marketing version. We have a clinical workflow that’s, like, very sensitive to output drift.

[00:27] Sam Ortega: And we need something we can explain internally, too. Like, what changed and why, and can we roll it back if it gets weird.

[00:35] Jada Williams: Makes sense. Maybe we start with definitions so we’re aligned. When we say “model version” in Redwood, it’s not just “the base model name.” It’s a specific artifact set: weights, tokenizer, serving runtime requirements, and a set of metadata around compatibility and known changes.

[00:52] Mark Liu: So it’s, like, a semver thing? Or is it a hash? Because today with Bedrock it’s a label, and with some hosted APIs it’s sort of implied “latest.”

[01:03] Jada Williams: Good question. Internally it’s backed by immutable identifiers, but customer-facing we’re moving to semantic versioning as the primary thing you see and pin to. The short version: you can pin to a specific version, you can choose a “track” like stable, and promotions are explicit events.

[01:21] Priya Natarajan: Promotions being, you push something to production?

[01:25] Jada Williams: Right. “Promotion” is: a model version becomes eligible or active in a given deployment mode. Hosted, Dedicated, Private can differ. Dedicated is usually more controlled and can be opt-in depending on your policy.

[01:40] Liam O'Rourke: And for you all, given you mentioned change windows, we’ve been steering healthcare folks into Dedicated with pinned versions plus controlled canaries.

[01:49] Alyssa Grant: Okay. So specifically: can we pin production to, say, version 1.7.2, and simultaneously do A/B traffic to 1.8.0 in the same endpoint? Or do we need separate endpoints?

[02:05] Jada Williams: You can do it either way. The cleaner pattern is: one “route” for production that stays pinned, and an experiment route that uses a rollout policy with a traffic split. Under the hood, it’s still your Dedicated capacity pool. The routing layer does the split.

[02:24] Mark Liu: So that’s basically like a feature flag but at the model router.

[02:27] Jada Williams: Yep. And the critical piece: each request is tagged with which model version actually served it. That’s what powers both the change history and the audit trail.

[02:39] Priya Natarajan: Tagged where? In logs? In an audit record?

[02:44] Jada Williams: In multiple places. For customer-visible: you can see it in Console request traces if you enable tracing, and in aggregated metrics. For compliance/audit: model metadata changes and promotions emit audit events with actor identity.

[02:58] Connor O'Brien: And just to separate: request logs are operational telemetry; audit logs are “someone changed config or promoted a version.” Different retention and export options.

[03:11] Sam Ortega: Our pain is when a vendor says “we improved quality,” and then suddenly our structured format breaks. How do you label that?

[03:21] Connor O'Brien: That’s exactly why we’re standardizing categories in release notes. “Breaking change” is reserved for changes that can reasonably break integration contracts: tokenizer changes, output schema changes if you’re using structured output, tool-calling behavior changes, or deprecations that remove prior behavior.

[03:39] Jada Williams: And we attach compatibility constraints in metadata. Like: requires tokenizer version X, or “incompatible with prompts expecting old system format.” We don’t say that verbatim publicly sometimes, but we can say “Potential formatting differences for JSON mode; review guidance.”

[03:55] Mark Liu: So you do have JSON mode? We’re using a lot of structured output.

[04:00] Jada Williams: Yes, structured output / constrained decoding depending on the model family. But the important thing is: if we change anything in that stack, it’s a release note event and typically flagged as higher risk.

[04:14] Alyssa Grant: Can you explain, like, the flow? What generates the release notes? Is it somebody writing a doc page manually? Because that’s where we’ve been burned—silent changes.

[04:25] Connor O'Brien: Historically, some of that was too manual. We’re moving to an automated changelog generator. The source is model metadata plus change events. When a model version is promoted, it emits an event. When metadata changes—like deprecation date, availability, safety notes—that emits an event. The release notes page is generated from those events with a template.

[04:47] Priya Natarajan: And who approves the wording?

[04:50] Connor O'Brien: There are approval gates for public notes when severity is high (breaking, security, deprecation). There’s also a CI check that produces a “release note preview” artifact during change review.

[05:03] Liam O'Rourke: The goal is consistency. You’re not at the mercy of someone remembering to update docs.

[05:09] Mark Liu: How do you avoid leaking internal info? Like if you mention a vulnerability.

[05:14] Connor O'Brien: There’s a “public vs internal” field separation. Internal notes can include incident IDs, internal service names, exact exploit details, customer-specific context. Public notes are templated and redacted. Console shows public notes to standard users; internal notes are RBAC-gated.

[05:33] Priya Natarajan: RBAC matters. We’ve had cases where support portals leak internal comments.

[05:38] Jada Williams: Totally. We actually had a UI regression a while back and added a test so internal fields literally cannot render to non-admin roles. The API also enforces it.

[05:50] Alyssa Grant: Okay. Dedicated specifics: if Redwood promotes a version, does it automatically start serving our endpoint? Or is there a control we own?

[05:59] Jada Williams: Dedicated gives you control. There are two concepts: “available” and “active.” Promotion can make a version available for your deployment, but your route can remain pinned to your active version until you change it or a policy rolls it forward.

[06:18] Mark Liu: So it’s like: you publish, but we decide when to switch.

[06:21] Jada Williams: Exactly. You can set a policy like “auto-advance minor versions after 7 days with no regressions,” or you can make it fully manual.

[06:32] Sam Ortega: We probably want manual for production, at least initially.

[06:36] Liam O'Rourke: That’s common for regulated. Then we usually set up canary on a smaller cohort, get confidence, then promote within your environment.

[06:48] Alyssa Grant: Let’s talk about rollback. What is rollback, technically? Is it just routing back, or do you roll back weights on GPUs?

[06:56] Jada Williams: Most of the time rollback is “routing rollback.” Meaning: the new version stays loaded or available, but the router sends traffic back to the prior pinned version. That’s seconds to minutes, depending on cache warmup.

[07:12] Mark Liu: That’s good. But if the new version uses different runtime kernels and you tuned batching, does rollback also revert those settings?

[07:21] Jada Williams: If those settings are version-scoped, yes. We treat quantization profile / runtime config as part of the served variant metadata. So when you roll back version, you roll back those required runtime settings.

[07:35] Connor O'Brien: And that’s another reason for the metadata schema. It’s not just a name, it’s a whole compatibility envelope.

[07:43] Priya Natarajan: What about auditability: can we show “we changed models at 2pm and rolled back at 2:10pm” and who clicked it.

[07:52] Connor O'Brien: Yes. That’s captured as audit events: “version promoted,” “route changed,” “rollout policy updated,” “rollback executed.” Actor, timestamp, and the before/after values.

[08:06] Alyssa Grant: Is that per-account? Like scoped to us.

[08:09] Jada Williams: Dedicated and Private are per-tenant, so yes. Hosted is more global but still has per-route events.

[08:18] Mark Liu: How do we consume it? Console only? API?

[08:22] Jada Williams: Both. Console for humans, and there will be API endpoints to query model metadata and release notes programmatically. Some customers pull it into their internal change management tools.

[08:34] Priya Natarajan: Can you export audit logs to Splunk?

[08:37] Liam O'Rourke: We can talk specifics, but generally yes—SIEM export via standard sinks. Connor can share the schema.

[08:45] Connor O'Brien: We also have retention knobs depending on tier. For Dedicated we can align with your retention requirement.

[08:53] Sam Ortega: On A/B testing—how do we measure quality? We don’t want Redwood to claim “better” based on some generic benchmark.

[09:03] Jada Williams: We agree. In the release notes, we’re careful with wording. We can include: “Updated serving profile reduces median latency by X% under Redwood benchmark,” and for quality we only include something if it’s statistically meaningful and we can describe it safely. Often we’ll say “No known quality regressions on Redwood eval suite,” or “Improved tool-call accuracy on internal eval set,” with caveats.

[09:28] Mark Liu: Can we attach our evals? Like use our prompt set.

[09:31] Jada Williams: Yes, you can run evals in your environment. What we’re building is the ability to attach eval run IDs to a model version metadata record. That’s more internal today, but it helps traceability.

[09:45] Connor O'Brien: And importantly, public release notes won’t show your private eval details. But you can keep internal notes in your tenant.

[09:54] Alyssa Grant: Walk me through a practical scenario. Let’s say we’re on “rw-guarded-chat” version 2.3.1 (making that up). Redwood releases 2.4.0. What happens?

[10:07] Jada Williams: Sure. Step 1: Redwood publishes 2.4.0 into the registry. There’s a promotion event that says: “2.4.0 is now available in Dedicated in us-east” or whatever regions. A release note is generated: category, severity, summary, links to guidance.

[10:27] Jada Williams: Step 2: In your Console, you’ll see “New version available.” Your production route stays on 2.3.1 because it’s pinned.

[10:37] Jada Williams: Step 3: You create a rollout or experiment: 1% traffic to 2.4.0, compare metrics, maybe compare “guardrail outcomes” if you have them enabled. If you see drift, you stop the rollout. If it looks good, you increase traffic.

[10:56] Mark Liu: And “stop the rollout” is just set traffic split back to zero.

[10:59] Jada Williams: Exactly. Then if you fully adopt, you change the pinned version to 2.4.0, or you let the rollout policy finalize and set it active.

[11:10] Priya Natarajan: When that switch happens, you emit an audit event.

[11:13] Jada Williams: Yes.

[11:16] Sam Ortega: And the release notes we see, are those global or specifically for our switch.

[11:23] Connor O'Brien: Two layers. Global-ish model release notes: what changed in 2.4.0 overall. Then your tenant change history: “Lattice route X changed from 2.3.1 to 2.4.0 at time T.” The second one is not a narrative release note; it’s an audit/change log entry.

[11:44] Alyssa Grant: That actually sounds right. We need both.

[11:48] Mark Liu: Let’s talk edge cases. Tokenizer change. If you change tokenizer, is that always a major version bump?

[11:56] Connor O'Brien: That’s the policy we’re aligning to, yes. If tokenizer changes could affect token counts, segmentation, or prompt behavior, that’s major or at least flagged as potentially breaking. The metadata includes tokenizer identifier and compatibility constraints.

[12:14] Jada Williams: Also, some quantization changes can affect output subtly. We categorize those as “quality/performance” and we include risk notes like “may change determinism at high temperature,” etc.

[12:27] Mark Liu: I appreciate the honesty. A lot of vendors pretend it’s identical.

[12:32] Liam O'Rourke: We’d rather set expectations and give you controls.

[12:37] Priya Natarajan: Another question: Dedicated implies isolation. Are you sharing GPUs across tenants?

[12:43] Liam O'Rourke: Dedicated is reserved capacity. So you get a GPU pool dedicated to you. There are burst options, but base is isolated.

[12:52] Alyssa Grant: Okay. If we need to do a canary, do we need extra capacity? Like to run both versions at the same time.

[12:59] Jada Williams: Usually yes, because you’ll have two versions loaded concurrently, at least partially. We can manage memory by unloading the old one after promotion, but during A/B you’re effectively running two. So we size capacity or use a staged strategy: smaller batch sizes, or run canary in off-peak.

[13:21] Mark Liu: That’s an important operational detail. With vLLM we’ve had memory fragmentation issues.

[13:27] Jada Williams: Yeah, we do continuous batching and KV cache management, but capacity planning still matters.

[13:34] Sam Ortega: On the release notes, are you including latency changes? Because we care about clinician experience.

[13:42] Connor O'Brien: Yes, performance is a category. We’ll usually say “median latency improved by X% on Redwood benchmark under specified settings,” and we include the conditions (sequence length, region, hardware class). We avoid claiming it for every workload.

[14:03] Alyssa Grant: That’s fair.

[14:05] Priya Natarajan: Security notes—do you ever publish security items as release notes? Sometimes those can’t be public.

[14:11] Connor O'Brien: If it affects customers materially, we’ll publish a security category note, but wording may be high-level. For Private or Dedicated, we can also provide customer-specific advisories under NDA.

[14:25] Liam O'Rourke: And if you have a strict change advisory board, we can coordinate with your change window.

[14:33] Mark Liu: How does deprecation work? If a version is deprecated, does it stop working? What’s the timeline.

[14:40] Jada Williams: Deprecation is metadata: “deprecated_at,” “sunset_at,” and guidance. For Dedicated, we don’t automatically flip you unless there’s a critical issue. We’ll warn in Console and via our account team.

[14:56] Sam Ortega: That’s important because we may need to re-validate.

[15:00] Alyssa Grant: Can we see the deprecation timeline in the release notes feed.

[15:04] Connor O'Brien: Yes. Deprecation is a first-class category, and it’ll show up in the model’s change history and in the release notes index.

[15:14] Priya Natarajan: Also, do you log who viewed the release notes? For audit?

[15:19] Jada Williams: We don’t generally treat viewing release notes as an audit event, but we can log Console access events at a higher level. The more important audit is who changed the route or approved the promotion.

[15:34] Mark Liu: On approvals: can we require, like, two-person approval for a route change.

[15:40] Jada Williams: Not fully in product today, but we support RBAC roles and can integrate with your internal process. Some teams do it via API: route changes only happen through a pipeline with approvals.

[15:55] Connor O'Brien: And we’re aligning our own internal release process with those same gates so promotions don’t bypass review.

[16:04] Liam O'Rourke: For the pilot, we can keep it manual and documented.

[16:09] Alyssa Grant: Okay. Let me ask a pointed question: We’ve had “silent model changes” with some providers where the model ID didn’t change but behavior did. Do you ever patch a version in place.

[16:23] Connor O'Brien: Our policy is no. Versions are immutable. If something changes—weights, tokenizer, runtime, quantization profile—it’s a new version. There are rare exceptions for purely metadata corrections (typo in description) but even that emits an event.

[16:42] Jada Williams: And that’s why you can trust that pinning to 2.3.1 means you get 2.3.1.

[16:48] Mark Liu: Love that.

[16:51] Priya Natarajan: What about region differences? Like you promote in us-east before eu-west.

[16:57] Jada Williams: That can happen. Availability is per deployment and region. Release notes include availability info: “available in Hosted in X regions; Dedicated by account; Private bundle version Y.”

[17:13] Sam Ortega: Private bundle? We’re not doing on-prem, but our compliance team asks about it.

[17:18] Liam O'Rourke: Not in scope for you today, but good to know the system supports it.

[17:24] Alyssa Grant: Can we see a mock of what the release notes look like in Console.

[17:29] Jada Williams: Yes, I can describe it and we can send screenshots. It’s basically: a Release Notes feed with filters (deployment mode, region, severity), and inside each model there’s a “Change History” timeline.

[17:44] Mark Liu: Does it show the diff? Like what fields changed.

[17:49] Connor O'Brien: Internal view can show a metadata diff. Customer view is more narrative: “what changed” plus links to guidance. We avoid dumping raw diffs publicly because it can leak internal-only fields.

[18:06] Priya Natarajan: That’s fine.

[18:08] Alyssa Grant: A/B testing. How do we compare? Do you have built-in metrics.

[18:13] Jada Williams: You’ll get token usage, latency, error rate split by variant, and if you enable tracing, you can sample outputs for evaluation. For deeper quality, you’d run your eval harness.

[18:29] Mark Liu: We have our own eval harness. But we’d like correlation with rollout phases. Like “incident starts when rollout went to 25%.”

[18:38] Jada Williams: Yep, we track rollout phase events. There’s a concept of “rollout step changed” and it can correlate with your incident timeline.

[18:50] Sam Ortega: So if clinicians complain, we can look at exactly what changed.

[18:54] Jada Williams: That’s the goal.

[19:00] Liam O'Rourke: Anything else you want to cover? Maybe we should get specific on your desired policy.

[19:06] Alyssa Grant: We have a weekly change window, Tuesdays 2-4pm local. We want: canary at 1% for a day, then 10% next change window, then 50%, then 100%. And we want an automated rollback trigger if error rate spikes or latency goes above threshold.

[19:27] Jada Williams: That’s doable. For quality drift you’d likely do manual checks, but latency and 5xx are easy.

[19:35] Mark Liu: For quality, we can run a nightly eval and we can decide.

[19:40] Priya Natarajan: And approvals—route changes can only be done by our platform team.

[19:45] Liam O'Rourke: Great.

[19:48] Connor O'Brien: One more note: release notes will show “risk level.” It’s not a guarantee, but it helps triage. Breaking/security/deprecation flagged high; perf/bugfix usually medium/low.

[20:03] Alyssa Grant: Good.

[20:05] Mark Liu: How do you determine “risk.”

[20:07] Connor O'Brien: It’s based on category, plus some rules in metadata: tokenizer changes, runtime changes, quantization changes, etc. And we allow manual override with justification.

[20:22] Priya Natarajan: Is manual override an audit event.

[20:25] Connor O'Brien: Yes.

[20:27] Sam Ortega: Okay. That’s actually very aligned with how we operate.

[20:33] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, to wrap: we’ll send you (1) sample policy config and screenshots, (2) a redacted sample changelog artifact so you can see the release notes structure, (3) audit log schema info and retention discussion.

[20:48] Alyssa Grant: Great.

[20:50] Mark Liu: Also, can you confirm the API endpoints exist? We prefer to automate. Even if it’s beta.

[20:56] Jada Williams: They’re in flight, but yes, we’ll share what’s available and what’s coming.

[21:03] Priya Natarajan: And we’ll send our SIEM requirements. We use Splunk.

[21:07] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. We’ll schedule the working session next week.

[21:12] Connor O'Brien: Thanks all.

[21:14] Sam Ortega: Thanks.
